head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Edge b → a: course a needs b first. `indeg[a]` counts unmet prerequisites
deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
Courses with no prerequisites go first
Records the course when it is taken; the list is the answer
Unlike Course Schedule I, we keep the order
return order if len(order) == n else []
A shorter order means a cycle, and no valid ordering exists

p: No. After taking 0, both 1 and 2 are ready; the queue's FIFO order picks 1 first, giving `[0,1,2,3]`, but `[0,2,1,3]` is also valid and an accepted answer. Any order in which every course comes after its prerequisites works.

blocks.h: Why does an incomplete order mean a cycle?
p: Courses on a cycle wait for each other, so their indegree never reaches 0, they never enter the queue, and `order` ends up shorter than `n`. For example with courses 0 and 1 requiring each other, the queue starts empty and the result is `[]`.

210.takeaway: Kahn's algorithm with the order recorded: BFS over zero-indegree nodes; a short result means a cycle.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: House Robber I on a straight street: two rolling variables `prev` and `cur`
Slices: the street without the first house, or without the last house
With one house the two slices are empty and would return 0, but the single house can be robbed

p: `nums = [2,3,2]`. The first and last houses are adjacent in the circle, so at most one is robbed. Two linear problems cover it:
bullets: Answer `max(3, 3) = 3`. Robbing both 2s is impossible because they touch.

blocks.h: Why do two linear passes cover every valid plan?
p: Any legal plan leaves out the first house, the last house, or both. A plan without the first house is a plan on `nums[1:]`; a plan without the last is a plan on `nums[:-1]`. Taking the maximum of the two optimal results therefore contains the best legal plan, and neither case ever robs both ends.

bullets: Time: O(n), two passes (slicing copies O(n)).
Space: O(n) for the slices, O(1) otherwise.

213.takeaway: Circular House Robber: run the linear solution twice, once without the first house and once without the last.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Backtracking over digits 1–9; `start` prevents reuse and reordering
Choose each digit at most once
Stop when k digits are chosen, then test the sum
Digits only increase, so once x overshoots all later x do too: `break`, not `continue`
Next digit must be larger than x (each used once)

p: `k = 3`, `n = 7`. Each row is a length-3 path that the search reaches (pruned branches never get there):

head: path
sum
outcome
rows: length k but sum ≠ n → reject
length k and sum n → record

bullets: Only `[1,2,4]` has digits that sum to 7.

p: The loop goes over increasing digits, so once `total + x > n` every larger x fails as well. Breaking skips them all. With `continue` the answers would stay correct but the loop would test every remaining digit uselessly.

bullets: Time: O(C(9, k) · k) at most, since only subsets of 1–9 are tried.

216.takeaway: Fixed-size subset search with ascending digits; break as soon as the running sum exceeds the target.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict value → most recent index where it occurred
Remembering the last position of each item
x in last and i - last[x] <= k
Always overwrites with the newest index, so later checks measure the smallest possible gap

blocks.h: Why only the latest index per value?
p: For a repeated value, the closest earlier equal element is the most recent one. If the most recent occurrence is farther than k, every older one is farther still, so remembering older indices adds nothing.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the dict. A fixed-size sliding window set of size k reaches O(k) space.

219.takeaway: Hash map of last-seen index: the nearest previous duplicate decides whether a close pair exists.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Node count of a perfect tree of height hl, with no traversal
Otherwise recurse; at least one subtree is perfect

p: Tree `[1,2,3,4,5,6]` (complete, last row partly filled):

blocks.h: Why is this faster than O(n)?
p: In a complete tree, equal leftmost and rightmost heights mean the subtree is perfect, so it is counted by formula. Otherwise one of the two child subtrees is perfect (it ends at the full level) and resolves immediately in the next call, while only one child continues to recurse. So there are O(log n) levels of recursion, and each level measures heights in O(log n).
The shortcut is valid only because the tree is complete. For a general tree, equal leftmost and rightmost heights say nothing about the shape in between.

222.takeaway: Complete-tree node count: compare leftmost and rightmost heights; if equal, use 2^h − 1, else recurse.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Double-ended queue with O(1) operations at both ends
Adds to the back of the queue
Moves the front element to the back (a rotation)
Peeks at the front; here this is the stack top

p: The queue's front (left) is always the stack top. Each push rotates the older elements behind the new one:

blocks.h: Why rotate on push instead of on pop?
p: After `push` rotates `len(q) − 1` items, the newest value sits at the front, so `pop` and `top` are plain queue operations in O(1). The cost is moved to `push`, which is O(n). The alternative moves the work into `pop` and `top` instead; either way one side pays O(n) because a queue can only remove from the front.

225.takeaway: Stack from one queue: after each push, rotate the older elements behind the newest one.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: `i` is the start of a run, `j` scans forward to the end of the run
Bounds guard placed first so the index is never read out of range (short-circuit `and`)
Jump to the first element after the run
Each element is visited once overall

blocks.h: Why is this O(n) despite the nested while?
p: The inner loop advances `j`, and then `i` jumps to `j + 1`. Every index is therefore scanned exactly once overall.
A single-element run (`i == j`) prints just the number, not `7->7`.

228.takeaway: Two pointers over runs: extend j while consecutive, emit one range, jump i past it.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Powers of two are positive; guards zero and negatives
Bit tricks usually assume non-negative input
Flips the lowest set bit to 0 and all lower bits to 1
Zero only if n had exactly one set bit

p: A power of two has a single 1 bit (`10000`); subtracting 1 turns it into `01111`, which shares no bit with the original, so the AND is 0. Any number with another set bit keeps the higher bits after the AND, so the result is not 0.
Without the `n <= 0` check, `0 & -1 == 0` would report `0` as a power of two.

231.takeaway: A power of two has exactly one set bit, so n & (n−1) == 0; remember the n > 0 guard.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Fast moves twice as far; when it stops, slow is at the middle
Finding the middle in one pass
slow.next = prev; prev, slow = slow, nxt
Standard in-place list reversal (save next, flip pointer, advance)
`a` walks the first half, `b` walks the reversed second half
Stops when the (shorter or equal) second half is used up; for odd lengths the middle node is skipped

head: phase
state
rows: second half read from the new head: 1→2

blocks.h: Why does comparing only `b`'s length work for odd lengths?
p: For `1→2→3→2→1`, `slow` stops on the middle `3` and the reversed half begins there: `1→2→3`. Comparing walks `a: 1,2,3` and `b: 1,2,3`, but `3` is compared with itself because after reversal the middle points back into the first half. Equal anyway, so the result is correct; the first-half pointer never needs its own bound.

bullets: Space: O(1). The copy-to-array version uses O(n).
The list is left modified (the second half stays reversed); restore it if the caller still needs the original.

234.takeaway: Palindrome list in O(1) space: find the middle with slow/fast, reverse the second half, compare.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Copies the next node's value into this node
Deleting without access to the previous node
Unlinks the next node, which is now a duplicate

p: List `4 → 5 → 1 → 9`, delete the node holding 5 (we receive only that node):
bullets: The node containing 5 was never removed. Its slot now holds 1, and the old node holding 1 was bypassed.

p: Normally deleting a node needs the previous node to repoint its `next`. The problem gives no access to it, so the trick is to become the next node (copy its value and its link) instead.

It cannot delete the tail node (there is no `node.next`); the problem guarantees the node is not the tail. It also changes which object holds which value, so any outside reference to the next node now points to an orphan.

237.takeaway: Delete a node you can't reach the predecessor of by overwriting it with its successor.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Staircase search: the corner where moves are decisive
Everything below v in its column is even larger, so the column is eliminated
Everything left of v in its row is smaller, so the row is eliminated
Stops when the pointer walks off the matrix

p: 5×5 matrix with rows and columns sorted ascending, target 5:

From the top-left, both moves go to larger values and the search cannot choose. The top-right is the largest in its row and the smallest in its column, so each comparison removes a whole row or a whole column. A binary search per row also works but costs O(m log n).

bullets: Time: O(m + n): at most one move per row plus one per column.

240.takeaway: Staircase search from the top-right corner: each comparison eliminates one row or one column.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Latest index of word1 and word2; −1 means not seen yet
Tracking the most recent position of two things
`elif` is fine as the words are distinct (this version assumes word1 ≠ word2)
Larger than any real distance; initial minimum

p: `word1 = coding`, `word2 = practice`:

For any occurrence of one word, the nearest occurrence of the other word is either the latest one before it or the next one after. Checking at every step against the latest index of the other word covers the 'before' side for each occurrence, and the 'after' side is covered when that other word is reached. So older positions are never needed.

243.takeaway: One pass keeping the last index of each target word; update the minimum gap whenever both are known.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Digit → what it looks like rotated 180° (0→0, 1→1, 6→9, 8→8, 9→6)
Lookup table for a fixed mapping
The mirror digit must be the rotation of the left digit
`<=` so the middle digit of an odd-length number is also checked against itself

p: For an odd-length number the pointers meet on one middle digit, and that digit must be its own rotation: `"8"` qualifies, `"6"` does not (6 rotates to 9). With `<` the loop would skip that digit and wrongly accept `"6"`; with `<=` it checks `pairs["6"] != "6"` and returns False.

246.takeaway: Two pointers from the outside in, with a rotation lookup; include the centre digit by using l <= r.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict that creates an empty list for a new key
A shift-invariant description of the string
Makes the difference wrap around the alphabet (a→z is 25, z→a is 1)

p: Each string's key is the tuple of consecutive differences mod 26:
bullets: `abc`, `bcd`, `xyz` all share `(1, 1)`; `az` and `ba` share `(25,)`; the single letters share `()`.

p: Shifting wraps `z` to `a`. In `az` the difference is `ord("z") − ord("a") = 25`, while in `ba` it is `ord("a") − ord("b") = −1`. Python's `-1 % 26` is 25, so both strings get the key `(25,)`. Without the modulo they would land in different groups although `ba` is `az` shifted by one.

bullets: Space: O(total characters) for keys and groups.

249.takeaway: Normalize each string to its sequence of letter differences (mod 26) and group by that tuple key.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sorts by start time (lists compare element by element), returning a new list
Next meeting starts before the previous one ends
Compares each meeting with its predecessor

p: `[[0,30],[5,10],[15,20]]` is already sorted by start:

blocks.h: Why do adjacent pairs suffice after sorting?
p: If any two meetings overlap, then some adjacent pair in start order overlaps too: if meeting A (earlier start) overlaps C, then B, which starts between them, starts before A ends (since C starts before A ends and B starts no later than C), so A and B overlap. Hence checking neighbours is enough.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy (O(1) with in-place `.sort()`).

p: The test is strict `<`, so back-to-back meetings like `[0,5]` and `[5,8]` are allowed.

252.takeaway: Sort by start time and check each meeting against the one before it; touching endpoints are not overlaps.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Stack of ancestors whose right subtree has not been entered yet (values decreasing from bottom to top)
Lower bound for all later values: the last ancestor we turned right at
A value below `low` would belong to a left subtree we already left
while st and st[-1] < x: low = st.pop()
x is bigger than the top ancestor, so we are going right of it; pop it and raise the bound

p: Popping an ancestor means the sequence moved into that ancestor's right subtree, so every later value must be larger than it. Any later value below the bound would have to sit in the left subtree we have finished, which is impossible in preorder. A counter-example is `[5,2,6,1]`: after 6 pops 5 and 2, `low = 5`, and `1 < 5` returns False.

bullets: Time: O(n), each value is pushed and popped at most once.
Space: O(n) for the stack (an in-place version reuses the input array as the stack for O(1)).

255.takeaway: Verify BST preorder with a monotonic stack plus a rising lower bound.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Special case: the digital root of 0 is 0
Maps any positive number to 1..9, giving 9 (not 0) for multiples of 9

p: Since 10 ≡ 1 (mod 9), a number and its digit sum leave the same remainder when divided by 9. Repeating the digit sum keeps that remainder until one digit is left. A positive multiple of 9 ends at 9, not 0, hence `(num − 1) % 9 + 1`.

258.takeaway: Digital root has a closed form: 0 if num is 0, else 1 + (num − 1) % 9.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: A tree on n nodes has exactly n−1 edges; fewer means disconnected, more means a cycle
Union-Find: each node starts as its own root
Follows parents to the root, with path halving (`parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]`) to flatten the chain
Both ends already connected, so this edge closes a cycle

p: `n = 5`, edges `[[0,1],[0,2],[0,3],[1,4]]` (4 edges = n−1, passes the first check):
bullets: No edge joined two nodes of the same component, so the graph is a tree.

blocks.h: Why is the edge-count check enough together with cycle detection?
p: With exactly n−1 edges and no cycle, the graph is a forest with n − (n−1) = 1 component, i.e. a single tree. So we don't need a separate connectivity pass. A graph with n−1 edges and a cycle must be disconnected, and the union-find finds the cycle edge: for edges `[[0,1],[1,2],[2,0],[3,4]]` on 5 nodes the third edge `(2,0)` finds both ends under root 2.

261.takeaway: Valid tree = exactly n−1 edges and no cycle; union-find detects the cycle edge.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The sequence built in order, starting with 1
Generating a sorted sequence from multiples
For each factor, the index of the smallest ugly number whose multiple is not yet in the list
Next ugly number: the smallest of the three candidates
Advance every pointer that produced the value, so duplicates such as 6 = 2·3 = 3·2 are generated once

p: `n = 10`. Each row shows the new number, the three candidates (×2, ×3, ×5) it was chosen from, and the pointers afterwards:
At value 6 both `ugly[i2]*2` (3·2) and `ugly[i3]*3` (2·3) equal 6. Both pointers must move, otherwise 6 would be appended again on the next step.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the list. A min-heap with a seen-set is O(n log n).

264.takeaway: Ugly numbers via three pointers merging the ×2, ×3, ×5 streams; advance all pointers that tie.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Compares tuples: smaller distance wins, and on an exact tie the smaller value wins (the problem asks for the smaller)
root.left if target < root.val else root.right
BST property: closer values lie in the direction of the target
Stops when you fall off the tree

blocks.h: Why can we ignore the other subtree?
p: If target < node.val, every value in the right subtree is ≥ node.val and so farther from the target than the node itself, so nothing there can beat the current best. The same argument applies symmetrically, and each step discards a whole subtree.

bullets: Time: O(h): O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) for a skewed one.

270.takeaway: Closest value in a BST: walk down toward the target, tracking the best node seen (tuple comparison breaks ties).
